title: Investigating Beyond Mind and Consciousness
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The Sixth Patriarch says: “Tell all who study the Way — you must strive and use the intention.”

inline.s: The Sixth Patriarch says: “Tell all who study the Way — you must strive and use the intention.”
The essence of Chan practice: to investigate before a single thought has arisen.
Q: What is the meaning of “investigating beyond mind and consciousness”?
A: To investigate beyond mind and consciousness is to investigate apart from thought:
to investigate before a single thought has arisen
. Venerable Elder Xuyun says:
“You must know that the true huatou is to be investigated before a single thought has arisen.”
(See further
Xuyun's Chan Teaching

What gathers and accumulates is called mind (xin); what deliberates is called intention (yi); what discriminates is called consciousness (shi). Among “mind, intention, and consciousness,” mind refers to the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna), intention refers to the seventh consciousness (the manas), and consciousness refers to the remaining six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness). “Mind, intention, and consciousness” are the eight consciousnesses that constitute the consciousness-mind: the ālayavijñāna, the manas, and the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousnesses.
The Song of Realizing the Way says:
“That which damages the Dharma-wealth and destroys merit is none other than this mind-consciousness; therefore the Chan school settles the mind
(therefore the Chan school must be free of the deliberating mind)
, and suddenly enters the power of the knowledge of the unborn
(suddenly enters the power of the knowledge and vision of the unborn and the undying)
(See further
Commentary on the Song of Realizing the Way

[Dharma-wealth (facai)] This is the counterpart of “worldly wealth,” and refers to the Buddha-Dharma. Because the Buddha-Dharma can nourish sentient beings and is the provision that sustains their life of wisdom, just as worldly wealth is a treasure, it is figuratively called the Dharma-wealth. [Damaging the Dharma-wealth (sun facai)] Causing the true Dharma not to appear before one. [Destroying merit (mie gongde)] Destroying merit, so that at most one can obtain only worldly merit. For example, giving alms while attached to form brings only the bliss of rebirth in heaven, and cannot lead one out of the six realms of rebirth. [Settling the mind (liao que xin)] Not using the consciousness-mind (mind, intention, and consciousness).

“Investigating beyond mind and consciousness” means to investigate apart from the operation of the consciousness-mind (mind, intention, and consciousness). (Regarding the operation of the consciousness-mind, see further the section “The Process of the Operation of the Consciousness-Mind” in
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
“Investigating beyond mind and consciousness” is what the Sixth Patriarch says in the Platform Sutra:
“Tell all who study the Way, you must strive and use the
intention
; do not, though you study the Mahāyāna gate, cling instead to the wisdom of birth and death.”

(Translation: Tell all who study the Way — when doing the practice you must use the intention (the manas); do not be one who studies the Mahāyāna gate, yet does the practice with the mind-consciousness (the consciousness-mind). See further
A Detailed Explanation of the Sixth Patriarch's Platform Sutra
.) Shide also says:
“Alas, I see the people of the world, throughout endless eons lost on the crossing; if they do not realize this
intention
, their cultivation is only toilsome in vain.”
(From the Collected Poems of Shide.)
[The wisdom of birth and death (shengsi zhi)] The consciousness-mind.
intention

” is the manas, also called the mind-root. The characteristic of the manas is constant deliberation, giving rise to a discriminating mind. “You must strive and use the intention” means: the manas constantly deliberates and grasps the phenomenal objects in the ālayavijñāna; the discriminating mind and wandering thoughts are always produced by it. So to practice Chan is to use the manas to investigate, blocking the flow of wandering thoughts beneath the root of intention so that it does not proceed; and right where it does not proceed, to behold one's original face.
Master Hanshan says:

“This above is the usual hammer and tongs of the old man Dahui, and its intent is simply to make you block the flow of wandering thoughts beneath the root of intention with the huatou so that it does not proceed, and right where it does not proceed, to behold your original face.
It does not teach you to ponder over the gong'an, to treat it as a mass of doubt, and to seek a definite answer.
(From the Dream Journey Collection
Showing the Essentials of Chan Practice.)

Throughout history, those practicing Chan have had a great misunderstanding — playing with the consciousness-spirit: taking one's own reckoning and deliberation to be genuine doubt, and using the mind-consciousness to conjure up a scene, then believing one has awakened. Thereupon they compose verses and write essays, take themselves to be a good spiritual teacher, and go about expounding everywhere. In fact, this is a heartbreaking matter: it misleads oneself and misleads others. When reading the Chan gong'ans, recorded sayings, and teachings, one must be extremely careful. The patriarchs say:
“Those who study the Way do not recognize the true, only because from the very beginning they have mistaken the consciousness-spirit
the consciousness-mind)
. From the beginningless eons it is the root of birth and death, and the deluded call it the original person.”
Q: How does one use the intention (the manas) to investigate?
A: For example, the Patriarch Dahui says:
“Just lay your intention upon the very place where there is nothing to be considered.”
Chan Master Yaoshan Weiyan says:
“Think the very thing that does not think.”
Chan Master Guishan Lingyou says:
“By means of the wonder of thinking in no-thought, turn back and think upon the inexhaustibility of the spiritual flame.”
(See further
Dahui's Chan Teaching
Master Hanshan says:
“If you can really apply the mind, fix your effort solely upon the time before a single thought is born.”
The Dream Journey Collection · Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou
.) Again he says:
“Only, within each thought, watch the place where the thought has not yet arisen.”
(See further
The Single Move of Being Free from Thought
Venerable Elder Xuyun says:
“You must know that the true huatou is to be investigated before a single thought has arisen.”
(See further
Xuyun's Chan Teaching
In
Investigating the Buddha While Reciting the Buddha
one finds a detailed account of how to investigate beyond mind and consciousness and thereby see the mind and realize one's nature.
Q: Since when one investigates the huatou the whole mind-consciousness is in use, to require both being free of the mind-consciousness and investigating the huatou — is that not a self-contradiction?
A: First of all, what must be made clear is that the phrase “investigate the huatou” is an abbreviated way of speaking; its full form is “the Chan of investigating the huatou.”

The purpose of the Chan of investigating the huatou is to see the mind and realize one's nature (to see through to one's own nature), and to see the mind and realize one's nature is the state in which one's true nature reveals itself when the subtle thoughts are momentarily stilled. Therefore, generally speaking, the Chan of investigating the huatou has three stages: the myriad thoughts returning to one; the one returning to nothing; seeing the mind and realizing the true nature. The myriad thoughts returning to one is the coarse thoughts being stilled; the one returning to nothing is the fine thoughts being stilled; seeing the mind and realizing the true nature is the subtle thoughts being momentarily stilled. If the subtle thoughts are stilled forever, then one fully realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts] The thoughts of the mind are of three kinds: coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts. For example, for a person reciting the Buddha, wandering thoughts are coarse thoughts, while the thought of Buddha-recitation is a fine thought. Usually, when both coarse and fine thoughts are stilled, that is called “no-thought,” which is what is generally meant by no-thought. Further, if the subtle thoughts also cease, that is the ultimate no-thought. Therefore, the meaning of the term “no-thought” must be determined from the context. The “no-thought” in “the original mind is without thought” refers to the ultimate no-thought.
[Subtle thoughts (weixi nian)] The subtle arising, ceasing, and flowing of the consciousness-mind; it is the mark of the ālayavijñāna. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
“When the bodhisattva's stages are exhausted
(the ten stages fully cultivated)
, and the skillful means are fulfilled, in a single thought he is in accord; the awakened mind first arises, yet the mind has no first mark
Because he is far from the subtle thoughts, he sees the mind-nature
, and the mind is ever abiding; this is called ultimate awakening.”
Master Guifeng says:
“If the subtle flowing
(the subtle thoughts)

is entirely quenched, only the great wisdom of perfect awakening stands alone in brightness, and then, responding to conditions, [the one] manifests hundreds of billions of bodies to save connected sentient beings; this is called being a Buddha.”
(See the Jingde Transmission of the Lamp.)

The process of cultivation is to still in sequence the coarse, the fine, and the subtle thoughts, returning from the state of the consciousness-mind to the state of the original mind. The myriad thoughts returning to one is the coarse thoughts being extinguished, with only the fine and subtle thoughts remaining. The one returning to nothing is the fine thoughts being extinguished, with only the subtle thoughts remaining. Seeing the mind and realizing the true nature is the subtle thoughts being momentarily stilled. Fully realizing the fruit of Buddhahood is the subtle thoughts being stilled forever, with only the great wisdom of perfect awakening standing alone in brightness.

Now let me use investigating the Buddha while reciting to illustrate. The huatou of investigating the Buddha while reciting is a single recitation of the Buddha's name: recite one “Namo Amitabha Buddha,” then investigate: Who is the one reciting the Buddha? If one uses the consciousness-mind to investigate, it suffices to answer with a single phrase “it is self-nature.” But can this lead to seeing the mind and realizing the true nature?

Therefore, the path to seeing the mind and realizing the true nature through investigating “Who is reciting the Buddha?” is this: first, accomplish the myriad thoughts returning to one, that is, all wandering thoughts gone, with only the single recitation of the Buddha's name (the huatou) remaining. Then, accomplish the one returning to nothing, that is, even the thought of the Buddha's name (the huatou) is gone, abiding in the state where not a single thought is born. Finally, in this state where not a single thought is born, continue to press forward and investigate fiercely (investigating beyond mind and consciousness); after a long time one naturally sees one's original face (one's true nature), and sees the mind and realizes the true nature.

Therefore, the Chan of investigating the huatou is not to think about and conjecture over the huatou, but to investigate apart from the mind-consciousness; the patriarchs of old have many teachings on this. The huatou is used only in the initial stage of Chan practice, to resist the never-ceasing, flying wandering thoughts (coarse thoughts). Once the wandering thoughts (coarse thoughts) are stilled and the myriad thoughts returning to one is accomplished, even the huatou (the tile used to knock at the gate) must be put down, and one enters the state where not a single thought is born,
investigating before a single thought has arisen
(investigating beyond mind and consciousness). For the whole concrete method of investigation, see further
Investigating the Buddha While Reciting the Buddha
[Even the huatou must be put down] The patriarchs compare the huatou to a tile used to knock at the gate. For example, Master Hanshan says:
“The ancients say that lifting the huatou in Chan practice is all a matter of necessity. Though the gong'ans are many, only the huatou of investigating the Buddha while reciting
(investigating “Who is reciting the Buddha?”)

gains strength very easily amidst the dust and toil. Though it gains strength easily, it is only like a tile used to knock at the gate; in the end it must be thrown away, only it cannot be dispensed with for a while.”
(From the Dream Journey Collection

Reply to Censor Zheng Kunyan.) [A tile to knock at the gate (qiaomen wazi)] Pick up a shard of tile from the ground to knock at the courtyard gate; once the gate is knocked open, the tile is cast away; “wazi” means a shard of tile.

Therefore, investigating the huatou (the Chan of investigating the huatou) uses the mind-consciousness only in the initial stage, and it is restricted to the appearance of only one thought — the huatou. As the practice deepens, the interval between one huatou and the next grows longer and longer, and in these intervals not a single thought is born. To “press and investigate” within this not-a-single-thought-born is precisely what is meant by investigating beyond mind and consciousness (that is, investigating apart from the operation of the consciousness-mind). Once one enters the stage of the one returning to nothing, there is no huatou either; it is entirely investigating beyond mind and consciousness.

From this we can see that investigating the huatou (the Chan of investigating the huatou) is not “the whole mind-consciousness in use.” To “both be free of the mind-consciousness and investigate the huatou (the Chan of investigating the huatou)” is not only not a self-contradiction, but the investigation of the huatou-chan is precisely to investigate apart from the mind-consciousness —
to investigate before a single thought has arisen; this is the very essence of Chan
